When Nike, Apple, and other major, trans-national companies can exploit labor laws in other countries, they will. They seek only to improve their own company's bottom line, however possible, if that means not paying a living wage to factory "sweatshop" workers, they'll do it. There's a good reason industrial manufacturing is dying in the United States, and it's because the labor protection and minimum wage laws that unions in America fought to pass, haven't been introduced in other countries.

Turns out it's starting to turn around, though.

There's a lot of talk of moving production back to the US because it turns out as shitty as US labor can be, it's still even better than what they're getting overseas. "You get what you pay for" works - at least somewhat - for the labor market, too. Surprise, surprise.

The cost is only part of it. Supply chain reliability is a huge factor. American labor has a habit of striking when they feel the employer is most vulnerable. This is usually when a business lands a large contract to supply government, or to supply components to another business. If you make washing machines, you are vulnerable not only to strike by your own employees, but strike by everyone who touches the product - suppliers, shippers, suppliers' shippers, etc. The answer? Move manufacturing to a place they don't strike.

The other factor is cheap imported labor - illegal aliens and H1B visa holders. 100% of the growth in employment since 2000 has gone to the foreign born. Semi skilled construction jobs that paid $15 an hour twenty five years ago, now pay $12 an hour or less. Technology industry & engineering wages are stuck at 2000 levels. Enforce immigration laws and stop issuing H1B visas, and wages will rise.

The 4 things that effect industrial economics.

  1. Raw Material Cost.

  2. Taxes.

  3. Utilities. (think electricity, water, etc)

  4. Labor.
